preachy

/PREE-chee/ - the stress falls on PREE · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Preachy means pushing moral advice or lessons in a smug, tiresome way — lecturing an audience on right and wrong when nobody asked for the sermon.

The reviews praised the documentary's research but called its narration preachy: every scene ended with the voice-over telling viewers exactly what to feel about it.

Example

Halfway through the novel the author turns preachy: the plot stops dead so a wise grandmother can deliver two full pages on gratitude, and the story never quite recovers its footing.

The lesson itself may be perfectly sound — gratitude is a fine thing — but preachy is a complaint about delivery: moral instruction pressed on an audience that came for a story, not a sermon. The suffix -y turns the verb preach into an adjective, 'characterized by preaching.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

moralizing: Moralizing means passing judgment on right and wrong at every opportunity; preachy adds the audience's fatigue — the lecture keeps going after it has worn out its welcome.

sanctimonious: Sanctimonious means making a show of one's own moral superiority; a sanctimonious speaker performs virtue, while a preachy one pushes advice — you can be preachy out of honest concern and still be tiresome.

didactic: Didactic means designed to teach a lesson — a didactic fable is simply doing its job; preachy is didactic gone wrong, the lesson delivered with a wagging finger nobody invited.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understated: making its point lightly, without insisting

nonjudgmental: offering no verdict on anyone's choices

Where it sits · how insufferable the moralizing gets

didactic → preachy → sanctimonious

didactic vs. preachy: Didactic is milder than preachy: a didactic story merely sets out to teach its lesson, while a preachy one keeps hammering the moral long after everyone has heard it.

sanctimonious vs. preachy: Sanctimonious goes further than preachy: the preachy narrator at least cares about the advice itself, while a sanctimonious one has moved on to advertising their own virtue.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — preach: to deliver a moral or religious lecture (Old French prechier, from Latin praedicare, 'to proclaim publicly')

Suffix — -y: characterized by; full of

Put it together: Preach + -y is this unit's suffix at its plainest: 'characterized by preaching.' Preach itself walked into English from Old French prechier, from Latin praedicare, 'to proclaim publicly' — prae- ('before, in public') plus the dic- root of dicare and dicere, 'to proclaim, to say.' That saying-root built a large family in English: dictate, verdict, dictionary.

Use the root in a new word: edict: By nightfall the duke's edict had been nailed to every church door in the province.

Root Check

Word Choice

disapproving / critical

Preachy is a critic's word — aim it at tone, never at content: a book can argue hard for honesty without being preachy, and a preachy one can still be right. It pairs naturally with laudatory, taught in this same unit: one voice drowns you in praise, the other in advice.
